extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of dramatic literature and playwrights studying Aristotle's Poetics and tragic craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating tragedy: how to construct a plot as the living principle of a play and how to shape character (éthos and dianoia) so that a hero's flaw and ensuing conflict produce pity and fear. Emphasises Aristotelian devices (peripeteia, anagnorisis), unity/necessity, and the relation of character to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic dyapria (primal defect / hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dyapria, the primal defect, is a frailty or flaw—'it may be human short-sightedness, it may be some error of blood or judgment'—whose virtues and strengths may nevertheless hurry the hero forward to ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This flaw need not be murderous intent; it can be an error of judgment or frailty that initiates the tragic chain. Examples: Othello and Oedipus (ruin wrought by noble characters with defects); Macbeth (ambition as taint). The dramatic interest often comes from tracing the growth of a frailty into crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious sin and innocent error both eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who innocently err are no less doomed than those who sin consciously; 'the tragic irony sometimes lies precisely herein' that virtues can lead to ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic protagonists may fall through innocent error as much as through conscious vice; both can produce involuntary guilt or expiation and elicit pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show causal chain from first fault to catastrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of the essence of a great tragedy 'to bring together the beginning and the end; to show the one implicit in the other' so that 'the first dyapria bears the weight of the tragic result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the plot so the initial flaw or false step is seen as causally connected to the final disaster; the intervening process should feel unified by necessity or probability rather than accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear, heightened to the utmost
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal tragedy 'will excite pity and fear in no ordinary combination, but these two emotions heightened to their utmost capacity under the conditions of the most perfect art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents and character arcs to maximize these emotional responses; evaluate success by intensity and purity of pity and fear produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex plot requires peripeteia (reversal) and/or anagnorisis (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'complex' tragedy is one in which the change of fortune is combined with Reversal of the Action (peripeteia) or with Recognition (anagnorisis), or with both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeteia: an intended action produces the opposite result (examples: Oedipus; Shylock; Haman/Mordecai). Recognition: knowledge changes from ignorance to awareness (example: Odysseus recognised by his nurse). These devices should be embedded in the plot's causal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot is first principle / the soul of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The plot is the first principle and as it were the soul of the tragedy.' The plot is the animating principle from which the parts grow and derive meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise building a unified, organic plot; without a coherent action there can be no tragedy. Use plot to reveal meaning; treat other elements as subsidiary to plot's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must represent a mode of human life (inner + outer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is 'an imitation of an action which is an image of human life — of its supreme welfare or misery; that life itself consisting in a mode of action, not in a mere quality of mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot should encompass both outward events (fortune/misfortune) and inward processes (motives, mental life). The action must reveal the inner sense of the characters, not merely record external happenings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and necessity/probability must govern plot and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of necessity or probability prescribed for the plot shall apply also to the speeches and actions of the dramatic persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure incidents and characters' choices arise from credible necessity or probability; avoid arbitrary turns that break the causal logic of the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethos (moral element) and dianoia (intellectual element) as components of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Éthos is 'the moral element in character'—an expression of moral purpose and permanent disposition. Dianoia is 'the thought, the intellectual element' implied in rational conduct. Together they constitute character and are causes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting characters, specify both moral orientation (éthos) and intellectual reasoning (dianoia). Show them through action and speech so that their choices feel grounded in both will and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethos and dianoia must be shown through action and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: In the drama characters 'enact their own story and so reveal themselves... We know them not from what we are told, but by what we see them do before our eyes.' Dramatic dianoia is often embodied in speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal moral purpose and intellectual motives via deeds that affect the plot and by speeches that contribute to action. Avoid telling or expository description unconnected to plot movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of character to plot (but not elimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle insists on the subordination of éthos to plot: 'Without action there cannot be a tragedy; there may be without éthos.' Yet in life and drama they exist together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give primacy to compelling action; character must serve the plot's necessities. However, do not reduce persons to mere types—distinctive traits that plausibly produce action are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'faultily faultless' heroes and consummate villains
rubrics_metrics.description: No 'faultily faultless' hero, any more than a consummate villain, can inspire so vital a sympathy as the hero 'whose weakness and whose strength alike bring him within the range of our common humanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create heroes with a mix of strengths and flaws that make them human and sympathetic; avoid idealised perfection or one-dimensional evil that fail to generate tragic pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show internal versus external collision of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The resulting collision may be: (a) an individual violating a known right and provoking external conflict, or (b) a collision between internal moral forces—'the struggles of conscience, the wavering purpose, the divided will.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the play's central conflict is primarily external (fate, other wills) or internal (moral struggle), and shape scenes to dramatise that collision authentically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must carry the thought; avoid relying on verbal exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be so shaped 'as to carry its message and meaning without the aid of verbal exposition... the pity and fear the poet desires to excite are conveyed by the inner structure of the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer showing over telling: make the story's structure communicate the poet's ideas. Speeches should illuminate or propel action, not replace it with explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid replacing plot with ethical monologues
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferior writers 'attempted... to make ethical monologues take the place of a well constructed plot.' Such monologues are 'preliminaries of tragedy' not the tragedy itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue for argumentative or rhetorical purposes only insofar as it advances action or reveals character; resist long rhetorical passages that stall plot momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (ironic reversal) as a source of tragic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia is 'a change by which a line of action intended to produce a certain effect produces the opposite—an overruling of the intention of one of the agents.' It is often nearest equivalent to the modern 'Irony of Destiny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineer reversals where an agent's intended means are co-opted by circumstance to produce their opposite, thereby intensifying tragic irony and pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (recognition) as another decisive device
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition (anagnorisis) is a means by which knowledge shifts and the plot's meaning is clarified (example: Odysseus recognised by his nurse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate discoveries that transform characters' understanding of themselves or events, ideally interlocking with reversal to heighten catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not aestheticize or 'ennoble' vice to the point of moral obfuscation
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Corneille: the notion that vice may be ennobled 'by aesthetic treatment' is misguided—'If we carry it out there is an end to all truth, and all delusion, to all moral benefit of tragedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying morally dubious actions or characters, do not conceal 'inner ugliness' such that the moral lesson or tragic deterrent effect is undermined. Maintain ethical clarity compatible with dramatic complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit degrees of tragedy: the ideal vs. inferior but interesting plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle concerns himself with 'what is best'—the ideal tragedy—but '..there may be an inferior, but still an interesting tragedy' which falls short of the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ideal as a guiding standard (complete complex plot, maximum pity/fear) but recognise legitimate variation; lesser forms can still be effective without meeting every Aristotelian precept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be revealed through enacted deeds, not description
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In the drama the characters are not described, they enact their own story and so reveal themselves. We know them not from what we are told, but by what we see them do before our eyes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatic scenes that make characters' dispositions and moral choices visible through behavior. Evaluate characterisation by how plausibly actions arise from the presented éthos and dianoia.
